rationale: Methods: the rate is count__domains__DISTANCE_TRAVEL/n_passages for each work (every work has exactly one passage). Early means year<1876 and late means year>=1876. I averaged works equally within each genre-by-period cell, took late-minus-early for each of the 8 genres, and averaged those 8 differences equally. Estimate: +0.052 passage-rate units (about 0.05 to 0.11 on average). 95% CI [0.032, 0.069] from 1000 bootstrap resamples stratified by genre and period. An author-cluster bootstrap gives a similar CI, [0.034, 0.069]. Robustness: the increase is positive in all 8 genres (+0.045 to +0.060). It holds within the UK, US and unknown origin groups and at every date-confidence level. Dropping low-confidence dates gives 0.055, keeping only single-edition works gives 0.049, and restricting to 1846-1905 gives 0.057. By decade, rates are about 0.05-0.07 from the 1830s to the 1870s, then about 0.11-0.12 from the 1880s on. That looks like a step change near the cutoff followed by a plateau, not a steady trend. Coverage: 6766 works from 1800 to 1920s, but the early period is thin (752 works), which widens the uncertainty; two early cells (domestic_realist, romance) have zero positives. Alternative explanations: changes in what was sampled or digitized after 1876, author-heavy clusters, the annotator tagging later language differently, and changes in genre definitions. The genre-balanced estimand and the author-cluster bootstrap reduce, but do not rule out, these explanations. The cited passages are tagged DISTANCE_TRAVEL in both periods; they illustrate what the construct covers but do not by themselves establish the trend.
